newsitem.title: USA: Gore urges TV industry to expand U.S. program ratings.
newsitem.headline: Gore urges TV industry to expand U.S. program ratings.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore urged the television industry Thursday to revise its aged-based system for rating programmes to include symbols signifying violence, sex and foul language.

The statement was the Clinton administration's first formal endorsement of such a move. It cames as negotiators for the industry and parent groups made progress on crafting a new system involving such references, sources familiar with the talks said.

"I remain hopeful that the television industry will decide to add V, S and L to the ratings, and that they will make sure that parents are given reliable information about the level of violence in Y-7 rated programmes -- the rating for acceptable programming for children over age seven," Gore said.

"In return, we think it is only fair that we allow sufficient time for the V-chip and the ratings system to work in America's homes," he added after meeting with parent groups and congressional leaders.
The V-chip is to be used in conjunction with the ratings and will allow parents to screen out shows.
Parental groups have argued that the existing ratings -- which includes TV-PG for parental guidance suggested -- do not go far enough in providing information about sex, violence and foul language.
Meanwhile, the Federal Communications Commission postponed a hearing scheduled for Friday into the current ratings, which were introduced at the start of the year.
The FCC wants to give negotiators time to strike an agreement on a new system that can then be put before the agency for its consideration.

"An agreement that will give parents more information about television programming to help parents make choices about what is appropariate for their children to watch is within our reach," Gore said. "Let's sieze the opportunity."
On Tuesday, Senate lawmakers gave the TV industry a week to develop a programme ratings system that satisfies parents groups or face legislation requiring changes.
